claim: A single i.v. injection of the MBP peptide protected against subsequent efforts to induce EAE by immunization.
source: A single i.v. injection of the MBP peptide protected against subsequent efforts to induce EAE by immunization (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A demonstrating protection from EAE following peptide injection.

claim: Donor T cells persisted in the spleen following PIT treatment.
source: Donor T cells persisted in the spleen (Figure 1B,C)
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 1B,C showing presence of donor cells in spleen.

claim: There was reduced production of IFN-γ and IL-17 in splenic recall assays amongst PIT-treated mice.
source: but there was reduced production of IFN-γ and IL-17, in splenic recall assays amongst PIT-treated mice (Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by cytokine measurement data shown in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: No evidence was found for an elevation in the frequency of Foxp3+ donor Tg4 cells in response to PIT.
source: Of note, we found no evidence for an elevation in the frequency of Foxp3+ donor Tg4 cells, nor in IL-10 production in response to PIT (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 1C showing no increase in Foxp3+ cells.

claim: No evidence was found for IL-10 production in response to PIT.
source: Of note, we found no evidence for an elevation in the frequency of Foxp3+ donor Tg4 cells, nor in IL-10 production in response to PIT (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by cytokine measurement data in Figure 1C showing no IL-10 production.

claim: A single exposure to the MBP peptide was sufficient for successful PIT without enhanced induction of cell death.
source: We concluded from these initial studies that a single exposure to the MBP peptide was sufficient for successful PIT, without enhanced induction of cell death, or establishment of Treg-mediated suppression, but rather an intrinsic unresponsiveness in the persisting Tg4 cells.
evidence: Based on inference from the experimental observations showing persistence of cells without increased death or Treg induction.

claim: PIT does not establish Treg-mediated suppression.
source: We concluded from these initial studies that a single exposure to the MBP peptide was sufficient for successful PIT, without enhanced induction of cell death, or establishment of Treg-mediated suppression, but rather an intrinsic unresponsiveness in the persisting Tg4 cells.
evidence: Based on inference from lack of Foxp3+ cell elevation and IL-10 production.

claim: PIT induces intrinsic unresponsiveness in the persisting Tg4 cells.
source: We concluded from these initial studies that a single exposure to the MBP peptide was sufficient for successful PIT, without enhanced induction of cell death, or establishment of Treg-mediated suppression, but rather an intrinsic unresponsiveness in the persisting Tg4 cells.
evidence: Based on inference from the combined observations of cell persistence, reduced cytokine production, and absence of Treg mechanisms.

claim: Splenocytes isolated from mice administered Ac1-9(4Tyr) were potent in vitro stimulators of a Tg4 T cell line beyond 72 hr after peptide injection.
source: Splenocytes isolated from mice administered Ac1-9(4Tyr) were potent in vitro stimulators of a Tg4 T cell line (Tg4.TCL) and remained so beyond 72 hr after peptide injection (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by proliferation assay data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: DC were more efficient presenters on a per cell basis than unfractionated splenocytes.
source: Whilst DC were more efficient presenters on a per cell basis than unfractionated splenocytes, B cells were very poor presenters (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by comparative stimulation data in Figure 2A.

claim: B cells were very poor presenters of peptide-MHC complexes.
source: Whilst DC were more efficient presenters on a per cell basis than unfractionated splenocytes, B cells were very poor presenters (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by stimulation assay data in Figure 2A showing minimal B cell presentation.

claim: The ability of DC to present the peptide-MHC complex in vivo was underlined by immunofluorescent staining showing transferred Tg4 cells in areas of the spleen rich in CD11c+ cells.
source: The ability of DC to present the peptide-MHC complex in vivo was underlined by immunofluorescent staining showing transferred Tg4 cells in areas of the spleen rich in CD11c+ cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence imaging data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The ability to stimulate the Tg4.TCL was only maintained in the CD4+ DC population.
source: The ability to stimulate the Tg4.TCL was only maintained in the CD4+ DC (Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by proliferation assay data comparing DC subsets in Figure 2C.

claim: CD4+ DC from steady state mice had particularly high expression of PD-L1 in comparison to other DC populations.
source: CD4+ DC from steady state mice had particularly high expression of PD-L1 in comparison to other DC populations (Figure 2D,E).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 2D,E showing PD-L1 expression levels.

claim: Transferred Tg4 T cells expressed high levels of PD-1 in response to PIT, in contrast to those from PBS-treated mice.
source: Transferred Tg4 T cells expressed high levels of PD-1 in response to PIT, in contrast to those from PBS-treated mice (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 3A,B showing PD-1 expression.

claim: Addition of an anti-PD-1 blocking antibody to ex vivo rechallenge cultures restored the ability of splenocytes from PIT-treated mice to produce IFN-γ and IL-17.
source: Addition of an anti-PD-1 blocking antibody to ex vivo rechallenge cultures restored the ability of splenocytes from PIT-treated mice to produce IFN-γ and IL-17 (Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by cytokine production data in Figure 3C comparing anti-PD-1 vs isotype control.

claim: Transferred naïve Tg4 cells from Tg4.PD-1−/− mice were insensitive to PIT.
source: Transferred naïve Tg4 cells from these mice were insensitive to PIT, going on to cause a typical course of EAE upon subsequent immunization that was indistinguishable from that induced with Tg4.PD-1+/+ cells that had not been subjected to PIT (Figure 3D).
evidence: Supported by EAE clinical score data in Figure 3D comparing PD-1+/+ and PD-1−/− cells.

claim: PD-1 plays a non-redundant role in this model of CD4+ T cell tolerance.
source: We therefore conclude that PD-1 plays a non-redundant role in this model of CD4+ T cell tolerance.
evidence: Based on inference from the observation that PD-1−/− cells are insensitive to PIT.

claim: PIT rendered the host mice profoundly resistant to disease in the passive EAE model.
source: PIT rendered the host mice profoundly resistant to disease (Figure 4A).
evidence: Supported by EAE clinical score data in Figure 4A.

claim: Teff cells persisted after PIT-treatment in the passive EAE model.
source: As with naïve T cells shown above, the Teff cells persisted after PIT-treatment, but importantly these cells failed to populate the CNS efficiently (Figure 4B).
evidence: Supported by cell count data in Figure 4B showing presence in spleen but not CNS.

claim: PIT-treated Teff cells failed to populate the CNS efficiently.
source: As with naïve T cells shown above, the Teff cells persisted after PIT-treatment, but importantly these cells failed to populate the CNS efficiently (Figure 4B).
evidence: Supported by cell count data in Figure 4B showing reduced CNS infiltration.

claim: PIT did not drive Foxp3-expression in Tg4 Teff cells in the passive EAE model.
source: PIT did not drive Foxp3-expression in Tg4 Teff cells (Figure 4D), nor was IL-10 production evident (not shown).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 4D showing Foxp3 expression levels.

claim: IL-10 production was not evident in PIT-treated Teff cells in the passive EAE model.
source: PIT did not drive Foxp3-expression in Tg4 Teff cells (Figure 4D), nor was IL-10 production evident (not shown).
evidence: Based on statement that IL-10 production was not observed.

claim: Within 4 days of PIT, proinflammatory cytokine production by the transferred Teff cells was profoundly diminished.
source: Rather, within 4 days of PIT, proinflammatory cytokine production by the transferred Teff cells was profoundly diminished (Figure 4E,F).
evidence: Supported by cytokine production data in Figure 4E,F.

claim: The loss of IFN-γ producing capacity in PIT-exposed Teff was not reflected in any loss in T-bet expression.
source: The loss of IFN-γ producing capacity in PIT-exposed Teff was not reflected in any loss in T-bet expression (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1 showing T-bet expression.

claim: An antibody to PSGL-1 can inhibit Tg4 Teff-driven EAE.
source: We have also found that encephalitogenic function of Tg4 Teff populations correlates with their elevated expression of PSGL-1 and that an antibody to PSGL-1 can inhibit Tg4 Teff-driven EAE (Figure 4G)
evidence: Supported by EAE clinical score data in Figure 4G showing effect of anti-PSGL-1 antibody.

claim: Transferred Tg4 Teff cells exposed to PBS showed elevated PSGL-1 expression.
source: Whilst transferred Tg4 Teff cells exposed to PBS showed elevated PSGL-1 expression, their counterparts that had been exposed to PIT showed PSGL-1 expression more comparable with that seen on the EAE-irrelevant CD4+ cells of the host mice (Figure 4H)
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 4H showing PSGL-1 expression levels.

claim: Tg4 Teff cells exposed to PIT showed PSGL-1 expression more comparable with that seen on the EAE-irrelevant CD4+ cells of the host mice.
source: Whilst transferred Tg4 Teff cells exposed to PBS showed elevated PSGL-1 expression, their counterparts that had been exposed to PIT showed PSGL-1 expression more comparable with that seen on the EAE-irrelevant CD4+ cells of the host mice (Figure 4H)
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 4H comparing PSGL-1 expression.

claim: Active PSGL-1 was reduced on Tg4 Teff cells in response to PIT.
source: Staining with a mouse P-selectin-human IgG fusion protein indicated that active PSGL-1 was also reduced on Tg4 Teff cells in response to PIT (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 4—figure supplement 2 showing active PSGL-1 staining.

claim: One consequence of PIT is disrupted PSGL-1-dependent T cell trafficking.
source: These data suggest that one consequence of PIT is disrupted PSGL-1-dependent T cell trafficking.
evidence: Based on inference from reduced PSGL-1 expression and CNS infiltration data.

claim: PD-1 expression was high on Teff cells retrieved from PIT-treated mice compared to PBS-treated controls beyond 2 weeks from peptide administration.
source: We also observed that PD-1 expression was high on Teff cells retrieved from PIT-treated mice compared to PBS-treated controls and that this difference was maintained beyond 2 weeks from peptide administration (Figure 5A–C).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 5A–C showing sustained PD-1 expression.

claim: Sustained PD-1 expression was not a consequence of any long-term pMHC presentation in the lymphoid system.
source: This was not a consequence of any long-term pMHC presentation in the lymphoid system, because PIT-treated Teff cells that had been retrieved from their first hosts maintained PD-1 (and did not induce EAE) when transferred into secondary hosts that were not exposed to PIT (Figure 5D–F).
evidence: Supported by secondary transfer experiment data in Figure 5D–F showing maintained PD-1 and lack of EAE.

claim: The tolerant phenotype was stable in T cells exposed to PIT.
source: The tolerant phenotype was therefore stable in T cells exposed to PIT.
evidence: Based on inference from secondary transfer experiments showing maintained tolerance.

claim: Tg4.PD-1−/− Teff cells were not tolerized and were able to cause disease in the presence of PIT.
source: As was the case with the earlier experiments using naïve T cells (Figure 3D), Tg4.PD-1−/− Teff cells were not tolerized and were able to cause disease in the presence of PIT (Figure 5G)
evidence: Supported by EAE clinical score data in Figure 5G comparing PD-1+/+ and PD-1−/− Teff cells.

claim: PD-1 is a required component of tolerance in the therapeutic setting using Teff cells.
source: As was the case with the earlier experiments using naïve T cells (Figure 3D), Tg4.PD-1−/− Teff cells were not tolerized and were able to cause disease in the presence of PIT (Figure 5G), also establishing PD-1 as a required component of tolerance in this more therapeutic setting.
evidence: Based on inference from the observation that PD-1−/− Teff cells are not tolerized by PIT.

claim: There were no gross differences in the numbers or frequencies of donor cells in PBS-treated hosts between Tg4.PD-1+/+ and Tg4.PD-1−/− Teff cells.
source: There were no gross differences in the numbers or frequencies of donor cells in PBS-treated hosts (Figure 5—figure supplement 1), indicating that PD-1 expression does not constrain the accumulation of donor cells in the absence of PIT.
evidence: Supported by cell count data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: PD-1 expression does not constrain the accumulation of donor cells in the absence of PIT.
source: There were no gross differences in the numbers or frequencies of donor cells in PBS-treated hosts (Figure 5—figure supplement 1), indicating that PD-1 expression does not constrain the accumulation of donor cells in the absence of PIT.
evidence: Based on inference from similar cell numbers in PBS-treated hosts regardless of PD-1 status.

claim: The PIT-driven elevation in donor cell numbers seen with Tg4.PD-1+/+ Teff cells was accentuated in Tg4.PD-1−/− Teff cells.
source: However, the PIT-driven elevation in donor cell numbers seen with Tg4.PD-1+/+ Teff cells was accentuated in Tg4.PD-1−/− Teff cells and a high frequency of these cells showed expression of the cell cycle marker Ki-67 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by cell count and Ki-67 expression data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: A high frequency of Tg4.PD-1−/− Teff cells showed expression of the cell cycle marker Ki-67 following PIT.
source: However, the PIT-driven elevation in donor cell numbers seen with Tg4.PD-1+/+ Teff cells was accentuated in Tg4.PD-1−/− Teff cells and a high frequency of these cells showed expression of the cell cycle marker Ki-67 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by Ki-67 expression data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: The frequencies of Foxp3+ Tg4.PD-1−/− Teff cells were reduced following PIT.
source: However, as seen with Tg4.PD-1+/+ Teff cells, the frequencies of Foxp3+ or cytokine+ Tg4.PD-1−/− Teff cells were reduced following PIT (Figure 5—figure supplements 2,3).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: The frequencies of cytokine+ Tg4.PD-1−/− Teff cells were reduced following PIT.
source: However, as seen with Tg4.PD-1+/+ Teff cells, the frequencies of Foxp3+ or cytokine+ Tg4.PD-1−/− Teff cells were reduced following PIT (Figure 5—figure supplements 2,3).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claim: PIT did not block the ability of Tg4.PD-1−/− Teff cells to produce IL-2 upon ex vivo re-challenge.
source: In contrast to their reduced effector cytokine production, PIT did not block the ability of Tg4.PD-1−/− Teff cells to produce IL-2 upon ex vivo re-challenge (Figure 5—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Supported by IL-2 production data in Figure 5—figure supplement 4.

claim: Tg4 Teff cells retrieved from PBS-treated mice had low expression of CD25 directly ex vivo.
source: Tg4 Teff cells retrieved from PBS-treated mice had low expression of CD25 and this was absent in their PIT-treated counterparts (Figure 5—figure supplement 5A).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 5—figure supplement 5A.

claim: CD25 expression was absent in PIT-treated Tg4 Teff cells directly ex vivo.
source: Tg4 Teff cells retrieved from PBS-treated mice had low expression of CD25 and this was absent in their PIT-treated counterparts (Figure 5—figure supplement 5A).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 5—figure supplement 5A.

claim: After 12 hr culture with MBP peptide, CD25 expression was increased in PBS-exposed Teff cells, irrespective of their PD-1-status.
source: After 12 hr culture with MBP peptide, CD25 expression was increased in PBS-exposed Teff cells, irrespective of their PD-1-status, but there was a notable impairment in this upregulation of CD25 in PIT-treated Tg4.PD-1+/+ Teff cells.
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 5—figure supplement 5B.

claim: There was a notable impairment in CD25 upregulation in PIT-treated Tg4.PD-1+/+ Teff cells after peptide stimulation.
source: After 12 hr culture with MBP peptide, CD25 expression was increased in PBS-exposed Teff cells, irrespective of their PD-1-status, but there was a notable impairment in this upregulation of CD25 in PIT-treated Tg4.PD-1+/+ Teff cells.
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 5—figure supplement 5B.

claim: The impairment in CD25 upregulation was not evident in PIT-exposed Tg4.PD-1−/− Teff cells.
source: This impairment was not evident in PIT-exposed Tg4.PD-1−/− Teff cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 5B).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 5—figure supplement 5B.

claim: The deficit in CD25-upregulation seen in PIT-treated Tg4.PD-1+/+ Teff cells was reflected by a low frequency of cells with phosphorylated STAT5 in response to IL-2.
source: The deficit in CD25-upregulation seen in PIT-treated Tg4.PD-1+/+ Teff cells was reflected by a low frequency of cells with phosphorylated STAT5 in response to IL-2.
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 5—figure supplement 6.

claim: PIT-treated Tg4.PD-1−/− Teff cells did not show abrogated STAT5 phosphorylation.
source: Notably however, PIT-treated Tg4.PD-1−/− Teff cells did not show such abrogated STAT5 phosphorylation (Figure 5—figure supplement 6).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 5—figure supplement 6.

claim: The ability of PD-1-deficient Teff cells to drive EAE despite administration of PIT is associated with their heightened capacity for clonal expansion.
source: We conclude that the ability of PD-1-deficient Teff cells to drive EAE despite administration of PIT is associated with their heightened capacity for clonal expansion.
evidence: Based on inference from the observed increased cell numbers and Ki-67 expression in PD-1−/− cells.

claim: Reduced frequencies of cytokine+ donor cells following in vitro restimulation were indicative of PIT-induced unresponsiveness in OVA-responsive Teff cells.
source: Reduced frequencies of cytokine+ donor cells following in vitro restimulation were indicative of PIT-induced unresponsiveness (Figure 5—figure supplement 7C,D).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 5—figure supplement 7C,D.

claim: PIT-exposed OVA-responsive donor cells showed higher levels of PD-1 expression than PBS-exposed donor cells.
source: Focusing on cells within the PD-1+ gate, PIT-exposed donor cells showed higher levels of PD-1 expression than PBS-exposed donor cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 8C).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 5—figure supplement 8C.

claim: Elevated expression of PD-1 associates with abrogation of effector function in response to PIT in a non-transgenic system.
source: We conclude that elevated expression of PD-1 associates with abrogation of effector function in response to PIT in this non-transgenic system.
evidence: Based on inference from the OVA system data showing PD-1 upregulation and reduced cytokine production.

claim: PD-1 is rapidly upregulated by T cells upon initial TCR stimulation but is then lost over time.
source: PD-1 is rapidly upregulated by T cells upon initial TCR stimulation but is then lost over time (Riley, 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Riley, 2009.

claim: Pathogenic Tg4 Teff cells expressed PD-1 on the day of transfer, but this was lost within 3 days of transfer in PBS-treated hosts.
source: This is exemplified by the fact that our pathogenic Tg4 Teff cells expressed PD-1 on the day of transfer, but this was lost within 3 days of transfer in PBS-treated hosts (Figure 5A,C).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 5A,C showing transient PD-1 expression.

claim: PIT drove the long-term expression of PD-1 by potentially pathogenic CD4+ T cells.
source: In contrast, PIT drove the long-term expression of PD-1 by potentially pathogenic CD4+ T cells and this was a required component of PIT.
evidence: Based on data showing sustained PD-1 expression in PIT-treated cells and requirement for tolerance.

claim: Sustained expression of PD-1 is important in CD8+ T cell 'exhaustion' in the face of chronic viral infection.
source: Sustained expression of PD-1 is important in another scenario in which T cells develop antigen-unresponsiveness; CD8+ T cell 'exhaustion' in the face of chronic viral infection (Barber et al., 2006; Wherry et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to Barber et al., 2006 and Wherry et al., 2007.

claim: CD8+ Teff cells with low PD-1 expression were reported to have elevated levels of the repressive H3K27me3 PTM at the Pdcd1 promoter, compared to either PD-1− naive cells or PD-1hi CD8+ cells from chronically infected mice.
source: Indeed, CD8+ Teff cells with low PD-1 expression were reported to have elevated levels of the repressive H3K27me3 PTM at the Pdcd1 promoter, compared to either PD-1− naive cells or PD-1hi CD8+ cells from chronically infected mice (Youngblood et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Youngblood et al., 2011.

claim: In naïve Tg4 cells and PBS-treated Tg4 Teff cells, neither H3K27me3 nor H3K4me3 was enriched at the CR-B and CR-C regions of the Pdcd1 promoter.
source: In naïve Tg4 cells and PBS-treated Tg4 Teff cells (neither of which expressed PD-1), neither modification (H3K27me3 or H3K4me3) was enriched at the two conserved regions, CR-B and CR-C (Youngblood et al., 2011), of the Pdcd1 promoter (Figure 6A,B).
evidence: Supported by ChIP-PCR data in Figure 6A,B.

claim: Both PD-1 expressing groups (Teff on the day of transfer and PIT-treated Teff) exhibited elevated levels of H3K4me3, but no enrichment for H3K27me3.
source: In contrast, both the PD-1 expressing groups (Teff on the day of transfer and PIT-treated Teff) exhibited elevated levels of H3K4me3, but no enrichment for H3K27me3 (Figure 6A,B).
evidence: Supported by ChIP-PCR data in Figure 6A,B.

claim: Functional (pathogenic) PBS-treated Teff that lacked PD-1 expression did not show elevated levels of the repressive H3K27me3 PTM.
source: Importantly, functional (pathogenic) PBS-treated Teff that lacked PD-1 expression did not show elevated levels of the repressive H3K27me3 PTM, thereby distinguishing their behaviour from that reported for PD-1lo CD8+ Teff cells (Youngblood et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by ChIP-PCR data in Figure 6A,B and comparison to published CD8+ data.

claim: It was not possible to distinguish PD-1hi pathogenic Teff from PD-1hi PIT-tolerized Teff based on their relative abundance of H3K4me3 versus H3K27me3 at the Pdcd1 promoter.
source: Moreover, it was not possible to distinguish PD-1hi pathogenic Teff (on the day of transfer) from PD-1hi PIT-tolerized Teff based on their relative abundance of H3K4me3 versus H3K27me3 at the Pdcd1 promoter.
evidence: Based on inference from the ChIP-PCR data showing similar histone modification patterns.

claim: CpGs within the CR-B region were largely modified (∼80% methylation across most CpG sites) in naïve CD4+ Tg4 cells.
source: Consistent with previous analyses of naive CD8+ T cells (Youngblood et al., 2011), CpGs within the CR-B region were largely modified (∼80% methylation across most CpG sites) in naïve CD4+ Tg4 cells (Figure 6C–D)
evidence: Supported by pyrosequencing and bisulfite sequencing data in Figure 6C–D.

claim: DNA methylation levels were considerably lower across the CR-C region in naïve CD4+ Tg4 cells compared to CR-B.
source: Consistent with previous analyses of naive CD8+ T cells (Youngblood et al., 2011), CpGs within the CR-B region were largely modified (∼80% methylation across most CpG sites) in naïve CD4+ Tg4 cells (Figure 6C–D), whereas DNA methylation levels were considerably lower across the CR-C region.
evidence: Supported by pyrosequencing and bisulfite sequencing data in Figure 6C–D.

claim: There were no differences in DNA methylation at the Pdcd1 promoter of pathogenic Teff cells on the day of transfer compared to naïve Tg4 cells, despite expression of PD-1.
source: Despite expression of PD-1 by Tg4 Teff cells on the day of transfer (Figure 5A), there were no differences in DNA methylation at the Pdcd1 promoter of these pathogenic cells compared to naïve Tg4 cells (Figure 6C,D)
evidence: Supported by DNA methylation analysis data in Figure 6C,D.

claim: Demethylation is not a pre-requisite for transient PD-1 expression following initial CD4+ T cell activation.
source: Despite expression of PD-1 by Tg4 Teff cells on the day of transfer (Figure 5A), there were no differences in DNA methylation at the Pdcd1 promoter of these pathogenic cells compared to naïve Tg4 cells (Figure 6C,D), indicating that demethylation is not a pre-requisite for transient PD-1 expression following initial CD4+ T cell activation.
evidence: Based on inference from the observation that PD-1+ Teff cells have similar methylation to naive cells.

claim: DNA methylation was maintained at CR-B and CR-C in the Teff cells retrieved from PBS-treated hosts.
source: As would be expected based on this result, DNA methylation was maintained at CR-B and CR-C in the Teff cells retrieved from PBS-treated hosts, where PD-1 expression had returned to levels observed in naïve T cells (Figure 5A).
evidence: Supported by DNA methylation analysis data in Figure 6C,D.

claim: PIT-exposed Teff showed complete demethylation at CR-C of the Pdcd1 promoter.
source: In marked contrast, PIT-exposed Teff, which had prolonged PD-1 expression (Figure 5A–F), showed complete demethylation at CR-C and significantly reduced DNA methylation at the CR-B region in the Pdcd1 promoter (Figure 6C,D).
evidence: Supported by DNA methylation analysis data in Figure 6C,D.

claim: PIT-exposed Teff showed significantly reduced DNA methylation at the CR-B region in the Pdcd1 promoter.
source: In marked contrast, PIT-exposed Teff, which had prolonged PD-1 expression (Figure 5A–F), showed complete demethylation at CR-C and significantly reduced DNA methylation at the CR-B region in the Pdcd1 promoter (Figure 6C,D).
evidence: Supported by DNA methylation analysis data in Figure 6C,D.

claim: Only PIT was capable of altering DNA methylation patterns at the Pdcd1 promoter.
source: Therefore only PIT was capable of altering DNA methylation patterns at the Pdcd1 promoter.
evidence: Based on inference from comparison of methylation patterns across different treatment groups.

claim: DNA methylation analysis enables PD-1hi tolerant cells to be distinguished from fully functional Teff, which only transiently express PD-1.
source: This enables PD-1hi tolerant cells to be distinguished from fully functional Teff, which only transiently express PD-1.
evidence: Based on inference from the distinct methylation patterns observed in tolerant vs. transiently PD-1+ cells.

claim: The first intermediate in the oxidation of 5mC is 5-hydroxymethylcytosine (5hmC), a stable epigenetic mark with widespread tissue distribution.
source: The first intermediate is 5-hydroxymethylcytosine (5hmC), a stable epigenetic mark with widespread tissue distribution (Kriaucionis and Heintz, 2009; Tahiliani et al., 2009; Song et al., 2011; Nestor et al., 2012; Thomson et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple publications establishing 5hmC as a stable epigenetic mark.

claim: Reciprocal changes for both 5mC and 5hmC at gene loci imply that demethylation may be occurring via a 5hmC intermediate.
source: Reciprocal changes for both 5mC and 5hmC at gene loci imply that demethylation may be occurring via a 5hmC intermediate (Thomson et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Thomson et al., 2013.

claim: Standard bisulfite conversion techniques cannot distinguish 5mC from 5hmC.
source: Of note, standard bisulfite conversion techniques cannot distinguish 5mC from 5hmC.
evidence: Based on established knowledge about the limitations of bisulfite conversion.

claim: There was considerable enrichment of 5hmC at the Pdcd1 promoter CR-B and CR-C regions in naïve Tg4 cells.
source: Using an affinity based technique (Thomson et al., 2012), we identified considerable enrichment of 5hmC at the Pdcd1 promoter CR-B and CR-C regions in naïve Tg4 cells (Figure 6E).
evidence: Supported by 5hmC DNA immunoprecipitation data in Figure 6E.

claim: 5hmC was present in Teff cells generated by 3-day culture, particularly within the CR-B region.
source: 5hmC was also present in Teff cells generated by 3-day culture (particularly within the CR-B region) and in Teff cells retrieved from PBS-treated mice.
evidence: Supported by 5hmC DNA immunoprecipitation data in Figure 6E.

claim: 5hmC was present in Teff cells retrieved from PBS-treated mice.
source: 5hmC was also present in Teff cells generated by 3-day culture (particularly within the CR-B region) and in Teff cells retrieved from PBS-treated mice.
evidence: Supported by 5hmC DNA immunoprecipitation data in Figure 6E.

claim: 5hmC was undetectable at CR-B and CR-C in cells retrieved from PIT-treated mice.
source: In contrast, 5hmC was undetectable at CR-B and CR-C in cells retrieved from PIT-treated mice (Figure 6E).
evidence: Supported by 5hmC DNA immunoprecipitation data in Figure 6E.

claim: All three known mammalian TETs were expressed in naïve CD4+ Tg4 cells.
source: All three known mammalian TETs were expressed in naïve CD4+ Tg4 cells, but these levels were substantially reduced in Teff cells (Figure 6F).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data in Figure 6F showing TET gene expression.

claim: TET expression levels were substantially reduced in Teff cells compared to naïve CD4+ Tg4 cells.
source: All three known mammalian TETs were expressed in naïve CD4+ Tg4 cells, but these levels were substantially reduced in Teff cells (Figure 6F).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data in Figure 6F showing reduced TET gene expression.

claim: Expression of each TET was partially restored in Tg4 Teff cells retrieved from either PIT or PBS-treated hosts.
source: Expression of each TET was partially restored in Tg4 Teff cells retrieved from either PIT or PBS-treated hosts, suggesting these that cells were equipped for the oxidation of both 5mC and 5hmC to occur.
evidence: Supported by qPCR data in Figure 6F showing TET gene expression levels.

claim: Tg4 Teff cells retrieved from PIT or PBS-treated hosts were equipped for the oxidation of both 5mC and 5hmC to occur.
source: Expression of each TET was partially restored in Tg4 Teff cells retrieved from either PIT or PBS-treated hosts, suggesting these that cells were equipped for the oxidation of both 5mC and 5hmC to occur.
evidence: Based on inference from the restoration of TET expression.

claim: Stable expression of PD-1 is coincident with demethylation of the Pdcd1 promoter.
source: Collectively our data indicate that stable expression of PD-1 is coincident with demethylation of the Pdcd1 promoter and that this requires a combination of permissive histone changes and oxidation of 5mC and 5hmC involving the activity of TETs.
evidence: Based on inference from the combined observations of PD-1 expression, demethylation, and histone modifications.

claim: Demethylation of the Pdcd1 promoter requires a combination of permissive histone changes and oxidation of 5mC and 5hmC involving the activity of TETs.
source: Collectively our data indicate that stable expression of PD-1 is coincident with demethylation of the Pdcd1 promoter and that this requires a combination of permissive histone changes and oxidation of 5mC and 5hmC involving the activity of TETs.
evidence: Based on inference from the combined observations of histone modifications, 5hmC loss, and TET expression.

claim: The combination of permissive histone modifications and TET availability only occurred in tolerant Teff cells following PIT, but not in Teff that transiently express PD-1.
source: In the system used here, these two requirements only coincide following TCR engagement in response to PIT.
evidence: Based on inference from the distinct patterns observed in PIT-treated vs. PBS-treated cells.

claim: A role for PD-1 in the establishment, or maintenance, of T cell unresponsiveness has been reported in various experimental models of autoimmune and allergic inflammation.
source: A role for PD-1 in the establishment, or maintenance, of T cell unresponsiveness has been reported in various experimental models of autoimmune and allergic inflammation (Probst et al., 2005; Cheng et al., 2007; Francisco et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple publications.

claim: Previous work had excluded a role for PD-1 in PIT-driven tolerance for naive CD4+ T cells.
source: Our previous work had excluded such a role for PD-1 in PIT-driven tolerance for naive CD4+ T cells, because PIT remained effective irrespective of antibody blockade or genetic deletion of PD-1 in the peptide-responsive T cells (Konkel et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Konkel et al., 2010.

claim: In previous studies using naïve T cells, PIT appeared to drive the abortive activation and apoptosis of peptide-responsive naïve T cells within 4 days.
source: In the two experimental models used in that study, PIT appeared to drive the abortive activation and apoptosis of peptide-responsive naïve T cells within 4 days, which would override any potential for PD-1-mediated long-term unresponsiveness.
evidence: Based on inference from previous study results cited.

claim: Teff persisted following therapeutic application of PIT, in contrast to previous studies using naïve T cells.
source: In contrast to those previous studies using naïve T cells, we found here that Teff persisted following therapeutic application of PIT.
evidence: Based on experimental data showing Teff persistence.

claim: Persistence of Teff following PIT is common to Teff with different inflammatory functions.
source: In a recent study using PIT to silence allergic airways inflammation, we found an analogous accumulation of allergic Teff cells, indicating that persistence following PIT is common to Teff with different inflammatory functions (Mackenzie et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Mackenzie et al., 2014.

claim: Transgenic expression of autoantigen on all DC subsets resulted in PD-1-dependent elevation in the frequencies of autoreactive Foxp3+ T cells.
source: A recent study transgenically expressed autoantigen on all DC subsets and found PD-1-dependent elevation in the frequencies of autoreactive Foxp3+ T cells as a result (Yogev et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Yogev et al., 2012.

claim: CD8+ DC can drive de novo Foxp3–expression due to their production of TGF-β.
source: That result may well have reflected an influence of CD8+ DC, which can drive de novo Foxp3–expression due to their production of TGF-β (Yamazaki et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to Yamazaki et al., 2008.

claim: CD4+ DC do not have the capacity to drive de novo Foxp3-expression.
source: CD4+ DC do not have that capacity, accounting for the absence of increased Foxp3-expression here, in Tg4 cells exposed to PIT.
evidence: Based on inference from the lack of Foxp3 induction and known properties of CD4+ DC.

claim: The predominant effect of PIT is to suppress pathogenic effector function rather than to drive gain of regulatory function.
source: This, together with the lack of evidence for IL-10 production in response to PIT suggests that, in this study, the predominant effect of PIT is to suppress pathogenic effector function rather than to drive gain of regulatory function.
evidence: Based on inference from the absence of Foxp3 and IL-10 induction.

claim: PD-1 has been reported to co-locate to TCR microclusters at the immunological synapse.
source: PD-1 has been reported to co-locate to TCR microclusters at the immunological synapse, where, following Lck-mediated phosphorylation of its ITSM, PD-1 recruits the SHP-2 phosphatase to counteract phosphorylation of TCR-proximal signalling machinery (Yokosuka et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Yokosuka et al., 2012.

claim: Following Lck-mediated phosphorylation of its ITSM, PD-1 recruits the SHP-2 phosphatase to counteract phosphorylation of TCR-proximal signalling machinery.
source: PD-1 has been reported to co-locate to TCR microclusters at the immunological synapse, where, following Lck-mediated phosphorylation of its ITSM, PD-1 recruits the SHP-2 phosphatase to counteract phosphorylation of TCR-proximal signalling machinery (Yokosuka et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Yokosuka et al., 2012.

claim: Inhibition of PI3K/Akt and MEK/ERK pathways can lower cell proliferation by reducing transcription of SKP2.
source: Inhibition of PI3K/Akt and MEK/ERK pathways can lower cell proliferation by reducing transcription of SKP2. This gene encodes a crucial component of the ubiquitin ligase SCFSkp2, which is required for cyclin-dependent kinase 2 activation and cell cycle progression from G1 into S phase (Parry et al., 2005; Appleman et al., 2006; Patsoukis et al., 2012; Pauken et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple publications describing this mechanism.

claim: SKP2 encodes a crucial component of the ubiquitin ligase SCFSkp2, which is required for cyclin-dependent kinase 2 activation and cell cycle progression from G1 into S phase.
source: This gene encodes a crucial component of the ubiquitin ligase SCFSkp2, which is required for cyclin-dependent kinase 2 activation and cell cycle progression from G1 into S phase (Parry et al., 2005; Appleman et al., 2006; Patsoukis et al., 2012; Pauken et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple publications.

claim: Exogenous IL-2 only partially restores cell proliferation by activating the MEK/ERK pathway but not the PI3K/Akt pathway.
source: Exogenous IL-2 only partially restores cell proliferation by activating the MEK/ERK pathway but not the PI3K/Akt pathway (Patsoukis et al., 2012), suggesting that IL-2 cannot reverse PD-1-dependent unresponsiveness.
evidence: Supported by citation to Patsoukis et al., 2012.

claim: IL-2 cannot reverse PD-1-dependent unresponsiveness.
source: Exogenous IL-2 only partially restores cell proliferation by activating the MEK/ERK pathway but not the PI3K/Akt pathway (Patsoukis et al., 2012), suggesting that IL-2 cannot reverse PD-1-dependent unresponsiveness.
evidence: Based on inference from the cited study showing partial restoration of proliferation.

claim: Recruitment of SHP-2 to the cytoplasmic tail of PD-1 is thought to function primarily by inhibiting the PI3K pathway.
source: Recruitment SHP-2 to the cytoplasmic tail of PD-1 is thought to function primarily by inhibiting the PI3K pathway (Chemnitz et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citation to Chemnitz et al., 2004.

claim: SHP-2 has been implicated in the dephosphorylation and inactivation of pSTAT5.
source: However, SHP-2 has also been implicated in the dephosphorylation and inactivation of pSTAT5 (Yu et al., 2000; Chen et al., 2003)
evidence: Supported by citations to Yu et al., 2000 and Chen et al., 2003.

claim: PD-1 signalling has been associated with a decrease in both the expression and phosphorylation of STAT5.
source: and PD-1 signalling has been associated with a decrease in both the expression and phosphorylation of STAT5 (Iliopoulos et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Iliopoulos et al., 2011.

claim: Inactivation of STAT5 can lead to a reduction in cell-surface CD25 expression.
source: Furthermore, inactivation of STAT5 can lead to a reduction in cell-surface CD25 expression (Kim et al., 2001).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kim et al., 2001.

claim: Inhibition of TCR signalling pathways by PD-1, coupled with inactivation of STAT5, would likely account for the impaired CD25 expression in PIT-exposed Tg4 Teff cells.
source: This, coupled with the inhibition of TCR signalling pathways by PD-1, would likely account for the impaired CD25 expression that we saw in PIT-exposed Tg4 Teff cells.
evidence: Based on inference from the observed pSTAT5 and CD25 data combined with known PD-1 signaling mechanisms.

claim: An impaired ability to upregulate CD25 is distinct from the classical profile for clonal anergy.
source: An impaired ability to upregulate CD25, and therefore to respond to IL-2, is distinct from the classical profile for clonal anergy, in which unresponsive T cells can upregulate CD25 but cannot produce their own IL-2 (anergy is broken by addition of exogenous IL-2) (Schwartz, 2003).
evidence: Based on comparison to established knowledge about anergy, supported by citation to Schwartz, 2003.

claim: An unresponsive state that blocks CD25 upregulation can be viewed as more secure than classical anergy, since it removes the risk of IL-2 from a bystander source overcoming that unresponsiveness.
source: An unresponsive state that blocks CD25 upregulation can be viewed as more secure, since it removes the risk of IL-2 from a bystander source overcoming that unresponsiveness.
evidence: Based on speculation about the functional implications of impaired CD25 upregulation.

claim: Teff that had been tolerized by PIT had an impaired ability to establish themselves in the CNS.
source: Consistent with their lack of encephalitogenicity, Teff that had been tolerized by PIT had an impaired ability to establish themselves in the CNS.
evidence: Based on inference from the reduced CNS infiltration data.

claim: Impaired CNS infiltration of tolerized Teff might reflect their impaired ability to undergo clonal expansion upon subsequent exposure to MBP in the CNS.
source: This might reflect their impaired ability to undergo clonal expansion upon subsequent exposure to MBP in the CNS, as discussed above.
evidence: Based on speculation about the mechanism underlying reduced CNS infiltration.

claim: A recent report indicated an additional role for PD-1 in inhibiting autoimmune T cell infiltration into the pancreas in diabetes.
source: A recent report has indicated an additional role for PD-1 in inhibiting autoimmune T cell infiltration into the pancreas in diabetes (Pauken et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Pauken et al., 2013.

claim: T follicular helper (TFH) cells are PD-1hi and PSGL-1lo.
source: T follicular helper (TFH) cells are PD-1hi and PSGL-1lo , but we do not believe that PIT drives Teff towards a TFH fate, since we did not observe any production of the TFH-associated cytokine IL-21, nor did we find evidence for any gain of the TFH-associated transcription factor BCL-6 following PIT (data not shown).
evidence: Based on established knowledge about TFH cell characteristics.

claim: PIT does not drive Teff towards a TFH fate.
source: T follicular helper (TFH) cells are PD-1hi and PSGL-1lo , but we do not believe that PIT drives Teff towards a TFH fate, since we did not observe any production of the TFH-associated cytokine IL-21, nor did we find evidence for any gain of the TFH-associated transcription factor BCL-6 following PIT (data not shown).
evidence: Based on inference from lack of IL-21 production and BCL-6 expression.

claim: The transcription factor T-bet can inhibit PD-1 expression in CD8+ cells.
source: The transcription factor T-bet can inhibit PD-1 expression in CD8+ cells (Kao et al., 2011)
evidence: Supported by citation to Kao et al., 2011.

claim: T-bet and PD-1 are not necessarily mutually antagonistic in CD4+ Teff cells.
source: but here we found that this was not the case for CD4+ Teff cells, which were T-bet+ PD-1hi following PIT, indicating that T-bet and PD-1 are not necessarily mutually antagonistic.
evidence: Based on inference from the observation of co-expression of T-bet and PD-1.

claim: The Pdcd1 promoter of Tg4 cells in their naïve state appears to be fully methylated, although this includes a significant level of 5-hydroxymethylation.
source: The Pdcd1 promoter of Tg4 cells in their naïve state appears to be fully methylated, although this includes a significant level of 5-hydroxymethylation.
evidence: Based on inference from the combined methylation and hydroxymethylation data.

claim: The presence of 5hmC, TET availability, and absence of repressive H3K27me3 histone mark suggests that the Pdcd1 gene is poised for transcriptional activation and PD-1 expression in naïve Tg4 cells.
source: This, together with the availability of TETs 1–3 and the absence of the repressive H3K27me3 histone mark, suggests that the gene is poised for transcriptional activation and PD-1 expression.
evidence: Based on inference from the combined epigenetic features observed.

claim: Early PD-1 expression following initial TCR ligation fits with the gene being poised for transcriptional activation.
source: This would fit with the known early expression of PD-1 following initial TCR ligation (as seen here in Teff on the day of transfer).
evidence: Based on inference connecting the poised state to observed rapid PD-1 expression.

claim: PD-1 expression during Teff generation was mirrored by chromatin changes associated with gene transcription (H3K4me3 enrichment), but without contemporaneous demethylation of the Pdcd1 promoter.
source: This PD-1 expression during Teff generation was mirrored by chromatin changes associated with gene transcription (H3K4me3 enrichment), but without a contemporaneous demethylation of the Pdcd1 promoter.
evidence: Based on inference from the combined histone modification and DNA methylation data.

claim: The considerable reduction in TET expression observed at the Teff stage should impede any active demethylation through the oxidation of either 5mC or 5hmC.
source: The considerable reduction in TET expression observed at the Teff stage should impede any active demethylation through the oxidation of either 5mC or 5hmC (a process that involves TET activity), thereby averting long-term PD-1 expression that would affect Teff function.
evidence: Based on inference from the observed reduction in TET expression and its expected functional consequence.

claim: Reduced TET expression at the Teff stage averts long-term PD-1 expression that would affect Teff function.
source: The considerable reduction in TET expression observed at the Teff stage should impede any active demethylation through the oxidation of either 5mC or 5hmC (a process that involves TET activity), thereby averting long-term PD-1 expression that would affect Teff function.
evidence: Based on speculation about the functional significance of reduced TET expression.

claim: In pathogenic Tg4 cells retrieved from PBS-treated hosts, histone modifications associated with active transcription are no longer evident.
source: As these cells transition to a PD-1-negative Teff state (pathogenic Tg4 cells retrieved from PBS-treated hosts), histone modifications associated with active transcription are no longer evident
evidence: Based on inference from the histone modification data.

claim: Although TET expression has been restored in PBS-treated Teff, the repressive chromatin state prevents the TET proteins from accessing the Pdcd1 promoter to allow demethylation.
source: and, although TET expression has been restored, this repressive chromatin state prevents the TET (and other) proteins from accessing the Pdcd1 promoter to allow demethylation.
evidence: Based on speculation about the mechanism preventing demethylation in PBS-treated cells.

claim: A key feature of the tolerogenic properties of PIT is to provide long-term PD-1 expression by tolerant CD4+ T cells.
source: However, a key feature of the tolerogenic properties of PIT is to provide long-term PD-1 expression by tolerant CD4+ T cells, which is associated with the presence of stable histone modifications characteristic of active transcription (thus enabling access of the TET proteins, amongst others), and therefore loss of both 5mC and 5hmC at the Pdcd1 promoter.
evidence: Based on inference from the combined observations of sustained PD-1 expression and epigenetic changes.

claim: Long-term PD-1 expression by tolerant CD4+ T cells is associated with stable histone modifications characteristic of active transcription.
source: However, a key feature of the tolerogenic properties of PIT is to provide long-term PD-1 expression by tolerant CD4+ T cells, which is associated with the presence of stable histone modifications characteristic of active transcription (thus enabling access of the TET proteins, amongst others), and therefore loss of both 5mC and 5hmC at the Pdcd1 promoter.
evidence: Based on inference from the combined histone modification and DNA modification data.

claim: Stable histone modifications enable access of the TET proteins to the Pdcd1 promoter.
source: However, a key feature of the tolerogenic properties of PIT is to provide long-term PD-1 expression by tolerant CD4+ T cells, which is associated with the presence of stable histone modifications characteristic of active transcription (thus enabling access of the TET proteins, amongst others), and therefore loss of both 5mC and 5hmC at the Pdcd1 promoter.
evidence: Based on speculation about the mechanism by which histone modifications facilitate demethylation.

claim: Analysis of the methylation/hydroxymethylation status of the Pdcd1 promoters may facilitate the discrimination of tolerant versus recently activated PD-1+ CD4+ T cells.
source: These data indicate that analysis of the methylation/hydroxymethylation status of the Pdcd1 promoters may facilitate the discrimination of tolerant versus recently activated PD-1+ CD4+ T cells.
evidence: Based on inference from the distinct methylation patterns observed in different cell states.

claim: Juvenile arthritis patients who responded to PIT using peptide from the DNAj antigen were reported to have an 'immune signature' that included elevated global PD-1 expression, relative to non-responders.
source: Juvenile arthritis patients who responded to PIT using peptide from the DNAj antigen were reported to have an 'immune signature' that included elevated global PD-1 expression, relative to non-responders (Koffeman et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Koffeman et al., 2009.

claim: The work on juvenile arthritis patients was based on assessment before undergoing PIT, rather than following PIT.
source: However, that work was based on assessment of the patients before undergoing PIT, rather than following PIT.
evidence: Based on description of the cited study design.

claim: It would be important to understand the relative expression of PD-1 before and after treatment in individual patients in future studies.
source: It would therefore be important to understand the relative expression of PD-1 before and after treatment in individual patients in future studies.
evidence: Based on speculation about future research directions.

claim: Analysis of the Pdcd1 promoter is needed to discriminate PD-1hi pathogenic Teff from the PD-1hi Teff rendered tolerant by PIT.
source: Furthermore, our study highlights the need for analysis of the Pdcd1 promoter to discriminate PD-1hi pathogenic Teff from the PD-1hi Teff rendered tolerant by PIT.
evidence: Based on inference from the distinct epigenetic signatures observed.

claim: Locus-specific DNA methylation-status would not prove a viable biomarker in itself due to technical challenges.
source: Therefore, whilst locus-specific DNA methylation-status would not prove a viable biomarker in itself, it might aid the identification of a surrogate phenotypic profile amenable to flow cytometric analysis.
evidence: Based on speculation about the practical limitations and potential applications.

claim: Locus-specific DNA methylation-status might aid the identification of a surrogate phenotypic profile amenable to flow cytometric analysis.
source: Therefore, whilst locus-specific DNA methylation-status would not prove a viable biomarker in itself, it might aid the identification of a surrogate phenotypic profile amenable to flow cytometric analysis.
evidence: Based on speculation about potential future applications.

claim: The demethylation of the Pdcd1 promoter seen in PIT-tolerized Teff is reminiscent of the changes reported to occur in CD8+ T cells exhausted in response to chronic viral infection.
source: The demethylation of the Pdcd1 promoter seen in PIT-tolerized Teff is reminiscent of the changes reported to occur in CD8+ T cells exhausted in response to chronic viral infection (Youngblood et al., 2011).
evidence: Based on comparison to published data, supported by citation to Youngblood et al., 2011.

claim: CD8+ Teff cells that transiently expressed PD-1 already have demethylated Pdcd1 promoters.
source: Youngblood et al reported that CD8+ Teff cells that transiently expressed PD-1 already have demethylated Pdcd1 promoters and their transition towards PD-1-negative memory cells is driven by the specific remethylation of their Pdcd1 promoters (Youngblood et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Youngblood et al., 2011.

claim: The transition of CD8+ Teff cells towards PD-1-negative memory cells is driven by the specific remethylation of their Pdcd1 promoters.
source: Youngblood et al reported that CD8+ Teff cells that transiently expressed PD-1 already have demethylated Pdcd1 promoters and their transition towards PD-1-negative memory cells is driven by the specific remethylation of their Pdcd1 promoters (Youngblood et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Youngblood et al., 2011.

claim: The methylation status of the Pdcd1 promoters within CD4+ Teff cells that transiently expressed PD-1 appeared unaltered from that of naïve CD4+ T cells.
source: In contrast, the methylation status of the Pdcd1 promoters within our CD4+ Teff cells that transiently expressed PD-1 appeared unaltered from that of naïve CD4+ T cells.
evidence: Based on inference from the DNA methylation data.

claim: It was only in the PIT-treated Teff that significant demethylation of the Pdcd1 promoter was observed, consistent with their sustained PD-1 expression.
source: It was only in the PIT-treated Teff that we saw significant demethylation of the Pdcd1 promoter, consistent with their sustained PD-1 expression.
evidence: Based on inference from the combined methylation and PD-1 expression data.

claim: It will be important to determine whether differences in Pdcd1 promoter regulation reflect intrinsic differences in how PD-1 expression is controlled in CD4+ versus CD8+ T cells.
source: It will be important to determine whether these differences reflect intrinsic differences in how PD-1 expression is controlled in CD4+ versus CD8+ T cells.
evidence: Based on speculation about future research directions.

claim: The appearance of 5hmC in the promoter of a key gene controlling T cell activation suggests that DNA hydroxymethylation may play a broader role in maintaining the 'pluripotent' state of naïve CD4+ T cells.
source: This is intriguing because the biological significance of 5hmC has chiefly been explored in the context of embryonic development. Its appearance in the promoter of a key gene controlling T cell activation suggests that DNA hydroxymethylation may play a broader role in maintaining the 'pluripotent' state of naïve CD4+ T cells.
evidence: Based on speculation about the broader significance of 5hmC in T cells.

claim: Global analyses to search for 5hmC and other intermediates of 5mC oxidation within the CD4+ T cell genome are warranted.
source: We suggest that this warrants global analyses to search for 5hmC and other intermediates of 5mC oxidation within the CD4+ T cell genome and also for the TET proteins with direct roles in the oxidation process (Deplus et al., 2013; Koh and Rao, 2013).
evidence: Based on speculation about future research directions.

claim: The Ac1-9(4Tyr) peptide of MBP is a potent tolerogen when administered in soluble form to wildtype H-2u mice or to Tg4 mice.
source: The Ac1-9(4Tyr) peptide of MBP, containing a Lys→Tyr substitution at residue 4 of the peptide, is a potent tolerogen when administered in soluble form either to wildtype (WT) H-2u mice or to Tg4 mice expressing a transgenic TCR responsive to this peptide (Liu and Wraith, 1995; Burkhart et al., 1999).
evidence: Supported by citations to Liu and Wraith, 1995 and Burkhart et al., 1999.

claim: B10.PLxC57BL/6 F1 mice are resistant to EAE induced with the MBP peptide, unless first seeded with a cohort of Tg4 T cells.
source: These F1 mice are resistant to EAE induced with the MBP peptide, unless first seeded with a cohort of Tg4 T cells (Ryan et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ryan et al., 2005.

claim: The CD4+ DC population is located in the T zone of the spleen.
source: The CD4+ DC population is located in the T zone of the spleen and so is ideally placed to present tolerogenic peptide to naive T cells (McLellan et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citation to McLellan et al., 2002.

claim: PD-1 contains an immunoreceptor tyrosine-switch motif (ITSM) that is thought to recruit SHP-2, a phosphatase that can inhibit the PI3K pathway.
source: PD-1 contains an immunoreceptor tyrosine-switch motif (ITSM) that is thought to recruit SHP-2, a phosphatase that can inhibit the PI3K pathway (Zhang et al., 2002; Chemnitz et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citations to Zhang et al., 2002 and Chemnitz et al., 2004.

claim: Signalling through PD-1 upon TCR stimulation has been shown to inhibit proliferation and the production of IL-2 and effector cytokines by T cells.
source: Signalling through PD-1 upon TCR stimulation has been shown to inhibit proliferation and the production of IL-2 and effector cytokines by T cells (Freeman et al., 2000; Sandner et al., 2005; Keir et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to Freeman et al., 2000, Sandner et al., 2005, and Keir et al., 2006.

claim: Reversal of unresponsiveness has been reported in CD8+ T cells upon blockade of PD-1 signalling.
source: Reversal of unresponsiveness has been reported in CD8+ T cells upon blockade of PD-1 signalling (Tsushima et al., 2007; Chikuma et al., 2009)
evidence: Supported by citations to Tsushima et al., 2007 and Chikuma et al., 2009.

claim: PD-1 was dispensable for both the induction and maintenance of tolerance in PIT-exposed naïve CD4+ T cells.
source: but PD-1 was dispensable for both the induction and maintenance of tolerance in PIT-exposed naïve CD4+ T cells (Konkel et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Konkel et al., 2010.

claim: PIT has been reported to reverse clinical signs of disease.
source: Although PIT has been reported to reverse clinical signs of disease (Leech et al., 2007), this scenario has been seldom explored mechanistically.
evidence: Supported by citation to Leech et al., 2007.

claim: PD-1 is transiently upregulated on both CD4+ and CD8+ T cells upon activation in order to restrain primary immune responses.
source: The co-inhibitory receptor PD-1 (encoded by the Pdcd1 locus) is transiently upregulated on both CD4+ and CD8+ T cells upon activation in order to restrain primary immune responses (Agata et al., 1996; Keir et al., 2006, 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to Agata et al., 1996 and Keir et al., 2006, 2008.

claim: The role of PD-1 in maintaining peripheral tolerance under steady state conditions is illustrated by the spontaneous development of autoimmune pathology in mice that lack PD-1.
source: Its role in maintaining peripheral tolerance under steady state conditions is illustrated by the spontaneous development of autoimmune pathology in mice that lack PD-1 (Nishimura et al., 1999).
evidence: Supported by citation to Nishimura et al., 1999.

claim: PD-1 is highly-expressed on exhausted CD8+ T cells.
source: PD-1 is also highly-expressed on exhausted CD8+ T cells (Barber et al., 2006; Youngblood et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Barber et al., 2006 and Youngblood et al., 2013.

claim: Peptide immunotherapy (PIT) is the subject of clinical trials in autoimmune and allergic disease.
source: Peptide immunotherapy (PIT) is the subject of clinical trials in autoimmune and allergic disease (Larche and Wraith, 2005; Larché, 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to Larche and Wraith, 2005 and Larché, 2007.
